title: Error Types at API Boundaries
concept: Absence, invalid input and contextual failure

writing.summary: An error type should preserve the distinctions the caller needs to handle.
writing.explanation:
A missing optional value and an invalid supplied value describe different outcomes. `Result<Option<T>, E>` can express success with absence, success with a value, or failure. The example converts `Option<Result<u16, ParseIntError>>` using `transpose`, preserving all three cases without manufacturing a default port.

At an application boundary you may add contextual information such as a safe field name or a public operation ID. Preserve a useful source error when appropriate and avoid depending on human-readable error strings for control flow. A library can expose typed error cases, while an executable may aggregate errors for reporting. Type erasure through a trait object trades some structured matching for flexibility and may need `Send + Sync` bounds if the value crosses task boundaries.

In an interview, begin with what the caller can reasonably do: retry, prompt for input, treat absence as normal, or stop. A retry policy also needs to know whether an earlier effect may have committed. Returning `Result` alone does not make a side effect transactional or idempotent. Do not leak credentials or private paths into a shared diagnostic merely because an error type can store them.
writing.exampleCaption: `transpose` preserves absence separately from a supplied value that fails to parse.
writing.rule: Choose error structure from caller decisions; absence, failure and defaulting are different policies.
writing.task: Explain the example, predict the result, and justify your answer to the follow-up.
writing.success: Identify the relevant ownership or API contract and test the changed constraint.
writing.question: Which outcome should `optional_port(Some("bad"))` produce under this contract?
answers: Ok(None), because every parse failure means the field was absent.
Err carrying the parse error, because the supplied value is invalid.
Ok(Some(0)), because Result automatically chooses a numeric default.
writing.feedback: `None` represents absence; malformed supplied input follows the error path. Defaults require a separate documented policy.

recall.question: Why is `fn optional_port(raw: Option<&str>) -> Result<Option<u16>, ParseIntError>` better than returning a default port whenever the value is missing or invalid?
recall.answer: It keeps three cases apart: `Ok(None)` means nothing was supplied, so the caller applies its own policy; `Ok(Some(port))` is a valid value; `Err` means the supplied value was invalid, so the caller can report it. A silent default would hide a typo.

recall.question: Why should callers not branch on an error's human-readable message, and what should go into error context at a boundary?
recall.answer: Message strings are for people and can change; expose typed error cases for control flow. Context should add safe facts such as a field name or public operation ID, never credentials or private paths.

depth.misconception: Ok(Some(0)), because Result automatically chooses a numeric default.
depth.correction: `Result` chooses no defaults. `parse` returns `Err` for `bad`, and `transpose` carries it out unchanged. A default needs explicit code such as `unwrap_or`.
